ARTICLE IN PRESS Motivating factors for young professionals involved in information systems projects Abstract Team members play a key role in the success of information systems (IS) projects. The literature on motivation tends to focus on IS professionals irrespective of their career stage. However, motivators seem to depend on the latter. Many young IS graduates leave universities to join IS project teams as external consultants (running the project from the IS consulting company’s side) S and function as key contributors to these teams. Therefore, it is imperative to understand the factors S that motivate these young professionals. Using a qualitEative approach, we surveyed master R students involved in a project-based learning courPse on IS projects. The results suggest that ‘personality traits’ (e.g., empathy and enjoymNent of interaction with others) can function as a I primary motivator for young team membe rs. ‘Role played’ also emerged as a new motivator. E L Therefore, our study provides a better understanding of what motivates young IS professionals, C I helping to improve project performance and IS education and training. T R Keywords: motivationA, young professionals, factors, projects, information systems. 1. Introduction Information systems (IS) projects are often complex undertakings (Hafseld and Hussein, 2021; Langseth and Haddara, 2024), as they involve the adoption of information technology (IT) in organizational contexts (Varajão, 2018). These projects are carried out by teams. To be successful, they need motivated and professionally competent team members (Newton et al., 2002; Othman et al., 2022). ARTICLE IN PRESS Individual motivation affects performance and is an important ingredient of project success (França et al., 2012; Hidellaarachchi et al., 2023). Most research on motivation tends to focus on professionals working in organizations adopting new IS (França et al., 2020; Hidellaarachchi et al., 2023), irrespective of their career stage. This research is valuable because demotivated workers may end up leaving the organization, while motivated workers will increase their productivity and stay with the organization longer (França et al., 2020; Othman et al., 2022). An IS classic project setup involves the IS-adopting organization, the system vendor, and the S external consultants who carry out the implementation (Haines and Goodhue, 2003; Ko et al., S 2005; Lech, 2013). Many young IS graduates leave universiEties to join IS project teams as external R consultants and function as key contributors to thesPe teams (Ko, 2010; Lech, 2013). Although motivators seem to depend on the IS professioNnals’ career stage, there is little research on the I impact of this contextual condition (Hid ellaarachchi et al., 2023). Therefore, IS consulting E L companies and academia need to understand better what motivates (and demotivates) these young C I professionals to improve their productivity and performance. T R However, studies based on these professionals’ perspectives are still limited. To fill this gap, we A used a qualitative approach to analyze data collected from a survey administered to master students involved in a project-based learning course on IS projects. Therefore, our sample is limited to one university (i.e., predominantly one culture group). Our findings indicate that ‘personality traits’ (e.g., empathy and enjoyment of interaction with others) can function as a primary motivator for young IS team members (e.g., in overcoming demotivating situations). They also suggest ‘role played’ as a new motivational factor for young professionals (in addition to those previously identified in the literature for IS practitioners in general). We are therefore contributing to the body ARTICLE IN PRESS of knowledge in this important area by providing new insights into the motivators of young IS professionals. In the next section, the background is presented. Next, the method is described. The following sections focus on the results, discussion, and contributions to theory and practice. Finally, the last section presents limitations and proposals for future work. 2. Background 2.1 Information Systems Projects S S IS are present in almost every aspect of business (VarajãEo and Trigo, 2016). This makes IS a R critical asset for improving efficiency in processes Pand transactions, reducing operating costs, N exploring new business models, or gaining competitive advantages, to name a few organizational I impacts (Meneses and Varajão, 2023; Vargas and Fontoura, 2024). E L IS projects are socio-technical unCdertakings carried out to improve an organization and achieve I business benefits (Varajão, 2T018; Varajão et al., 2019). An IS project is a temporary endeavor R undertaken to create aA unique product, service, or result. It can assume many forms, such as the deployment of commercial off-the-shelf applications or consultancy assignments (Varajão et al., 2022). Organizations are increasingly undertaking more complex IS projects to achieve their goals (Varajão and Takagi, 2024). The demands on IS professionals’ knowledge, skills, and performance (e.g., related to redefining business processes and tasks in response to the organization’s strategic initiatives) make it impossible for them to work independently. Therefore, IS project teams are formed with the purpose of creating innovative IS solutions (e.g., implementing advanced enterprise resource planning systems). These teams comprise business and IS specialists (e.g., external consultants ARTICLE IN PRESS and key users), selected for their ability to accomplish a given set of tasks within a limited timeframe, and are led by IS project managers (Lech, 2014; Moura et al., 2021). External consultants (from consulting companies, not necessarily system vendors) are hired when the IS-adopting organization does not have the internal knowledge and skills (nor the incentive to acquire them internally) to successfully implement an IS project (e.g., due to the one-time nature and complexity of the project). In the role of project manager, mentor/trainer, or technical implementation assistant, the external consultant (as a source of knowledge) can provide the S adopting organization with technical and business expertise, reduce the learning curve, configure S appropriate systems, and train users to take full advantagEe of the technology (Ko, 2010; Lech, R 2013). P N All IS project team members must keep up with new IT and adapt to new domains. Thus, for IS I professionals to succeed in this dynamic Eenvironment, they need to acquire new professional skills L on an ongoing basis, as the existinCg skills quickly become obsolete (Newton et al., 2002). In this I context, and also because of tThe overly aggressive competition between IS consulting companies, R the latter are constantly recruiting and training young IS graduates. As external consultants, these A professionals play a key role. For example, they can absorb enough organization-specific knowledge more easily to combine it with the system knowledge and contribute to an appropriate IS project design (Ko, 2010; Lech, 2013). In addition, most IS professionals need to be involved in challenging work using advanced technology. This environment allows them to develop professionally and provides training and technological development opportunities. For example, if IS consulting companies do not provide these conditions, young individuals may feel dissatisfied, demotivated, and more likely to leave the company (Warrier and Prasad, 2018). ARTICLE IN PRESS 2.2 Motivation The study of motivation is complex since a diverse set of environmental conditions influences it and can be moderated by factors such as an individual’s personality, values, and needs (França et al., 2020; Verner et al., 2014; Hidellaarachchi et al., 2023). Motivation is difficult to manage. Yet it is considered the single most influential factor in individual productivity (Verner et al., 2014; Othman et al., 2022; Demerouti and Bakker, 2023), so organizations cannot afford to ignore it. Motivation can be defined as a set of factors or events that energize, channel, and sustain human S behavior over time. A motivated individual at work will strSive to support the organization in E achieving its goals while satisfying their individual needs (França et al., 2020; Hidellaarachchi et R P al., 2023). N Motivation can be intrinsic or extrinsic. IntrIinsic motivation relates to an individual’s drive to E perform an activity to gain satisfaction through participation in it or to satisfy their moral and L C ethical values. In this case, individuals are motivated by the desire for competence, to perform I T important work, and to have autonomy or freedom. Intrinsic motivation has been positively R A associated with employee performance. Extrinsic motivation refers to the effort made by individuals to achieve rewards and recognition (e.g., financial incentives, career development, prestige, status, and positive evaluations from others in the organization) while avoiding negative consequences such as punishment. This motivation is associated with tangible rewards that should compensate for the lack of fulfillment and enjoyment of work. Although extrinsic motivators are quite important, autonomous behavior by employees is more often caused and initiated by intrinsic factors. Both intrinsic and extrinsic motivation influence employees to be more productive (Huck- fries et al., 2021; Othman et al., 2022). ARTICLE IN PRESS Although identifying consensual motivators is a major challenge, the extant literature suggests several that contribute to employee motivation. Some of these factors, suggested by Dwivedula and Bredillet (2010) and supported by recent studies, include professional/career development (e.g., related to the satisfaction of esteem needs) (França et al., 2020; Othman et al., 2022; Hidellaarachchi et al., 2023), work environment (e.g., reflecting the individuals’ expectation of working in a favorable environment) (Verner et al., 2014; Demerouti and Bakker, 2023), engagement of co-workers (e.g., a highly or poorly motivated team member may contaminate others) (França et al., 2020), well-defined work (e.g., to provide grSeater clarity about the objectives S of each activity) (França et al., 2020; Othman et al., 2022; Hidellaarachchi et al., 2023) and job E R security (e.g., allowing employees to show their true value to the organization) (Demerouti and P Bakker, 2023). The motivation to deliver unique products/services reflects these factors. As a N I result, IS consulting companies must effectively manage young professional motivators if these E external consultants are to contribute Lto the goals of the hiring organizations. C I In essence, motivation is a phenomenon that can encourage young people to work hard (e.g., as T R external consultants) to improve the performance of the IS-adopting organization (Muktiatun et A al., 2020; Othman et al., 2022). Furthermore, the motivation of these professionals can contribute to an increased probability of project success (Salman et al., 2021). Since the literature on factors that motivate young IS professionals is scarce, we searched the existing literature to identify factors that can motivate professionals working on projects. Method E L C Over the years, several individual motivation factors affecting IS project team members have been I T identified. For some authors (e.g., França et al., 2020; Hidellaarachchi et al., 2023), challenging R A work (although too little or too much challenge, such as the COVID-19 pandemic, seems ineffective in engaging employees (Nwoko and Yazdani, 2022; Demerouti and Bakker, 2023)), leadership (e.g., team leader and top management strategies) and professional/career development are important factors in individual motivation for IS project team members. However, these motivators seem to depend on the work context (e.g., the project domain, individuals’ role in the project, and their career stage). The impact of these contextual conditions needs to be further explored. For example, professional/career development seems to motivate mainly young IS professionals (i.e., with less than 10 years of experience in the IS field) (Hidellaarachchi et al., 2023). To fill this gap, this paper has the following research questions: What factors can influence ARTICLE IN PRESS the motivation of young IS project team members? How do these factors influence their motivation? 3.1 Data Collection To answer the research questions, we conducted an extensive survey of IS projects carried out in an academic context that follows a qualitative approach (Yin, 2017). We used a questionnaire- based survey designed to gather data on team members’ perceptions of the factors influencing motivation at both the team and individual levels. Therefore, it included the following open S questions: (1) “What did you like most about the project and wShy?”; (2) “What did you like least E about the project and why?”; (3) “In your opinion, wRhat contributed the most to your team’s P performance?”; (4) “In your opinion, what harmed your team’s performance the most?”; (5) “In N your opinion, what contributed the most toI your individual performance?”; and (6) “In your E opinion, what harmed your individual performance the most?”. The answers obtained are rich in L C content that addresses motivators, demotivators, and performance aspects at the team and I T individual levels. Our analysis focused only on team members’ perceptions of the factors R A influencing motivation at an individual level, involving a filtering process of relevant data to answer the research questions. We administered this survey to self-selected teams of students enrolled in the “Information Systems and Technology Project” one-semester course. This is a course unit from the fourth year of the integrated master’s in engineering and information systems management at the University of Minho. In this course, teams of three to six members were involved in developing a semester- long IS project (lasting, on average, three months) in a realistic work context (e.g., project customers were internal or external entities that received and tested the projects’ outputs). In each team, there was always a member with the project manager role. ARTICLE IN PRESS Before administering the survey, we conducted a focus group with five team members to assess the face validity of the survey. Results indicated minor refinements (e.g., rephrasing one of the survey’s questions to improve readability). These refinements did not affect construct validity. Next, from 2014 to 2023, we contacted several team members, inviting them to participate in the survey. A total of 955 participants were asked to complete and return the survey. Out of the 944 surveys that we received, we could not use 13 because of incomplete responses. Therefore, the 931 responses in our analysis represent a final response rate of 97.5 percent. 30.5 percent of the respondents were female, and the majority (58.4%) were betweeSn 21 and 22 years old. At least S one “crisis” situation occurred per year (either due to a member leaving the team prematurely E R because of internal conflicts or team members’ underperformance or due to the COVID-19 P pandemic situation in some years). Most teams had at least two members who had already worked N I together before on other projects. The projects included custom development, information systems E analysis, consulting, and others (businLess intelligence, workflow systems, etc.). C I The survey was successfully completed by 931 team members from different years: 116 responses T R in 2014/2015, 118 responses in 2015/2016, 114 responses in 2018/2019, 105 responses in A 2019/2020 (corresponding to four datasets from projects conducted in-person before the COVID- 19 pandemic), 144 responses in 2020/2021, 153 responses in 2021/2022 (corresponding to two datasets from projects conducted remotely during the pandemic), and 181 responses in 2022/2023 (corresponding to one dataset from projects conducted in-person after the pandemic). By collecting data from different teams and years, we minimized the bias caused by possible specific team characteristics. This allowed us to get complete and reliable results. The questionnaire was operationalized using the tool Google Forms. The standards of the Code of Ethical Conduct defined by the University of Minho’s Ethics Council were taken into account and respected during the study. Discussion L C Beyond the identification of new factors, such as the role played (in the project), it was possible to I T confirm that several motivation factors identified in the literature are also important for young R professionals, such as Arewards and incentives (e.g., Hidellaarachchi et al., 2023; Muktiatun et al., 2020; França et al., 2020), good work environment (Verner et al., 2014; França et al., 2012; Dwivedula and Bredillet, 2010), engagement of co-workers (e.g., França et al., 2020; França et al., 2011; Dwivedula and Bredillet, 2010) and well-defined work (e.g., Hidellaarachchi et al., 2023; França et al., 2020; Dwivedula and Bredillet, 2010), to mention a few. The theoretical and practical implications are discussed in the next subsections. ARTICLE IN PRESS 5.1 Contributions to theory The extant literature suggests that only the general understanding of the factors influencing the motivation of IS professionals has evolved. However, these motivators differ depending on the stage of the professional’s career. For example, ‘professional/career development’ seems to motivate mainly young IS professionals (i.e., with less than 10 years of experience in the IS field). However, research on these professionals has not advanced significantly in recent years (Hidellaarachchi et al., 2023). So, this study expands the existing knowledge about what motivates S the young members of an IS project team. Our study confirms previously identified motivational S E factors and identifies new ones, extending the existing knowledge body in this important area. R P At the individual level, motivation factors such as work support, a good working environment, N effective communication, learning, and application of skills had already been identified in the I literature and were also confirmed in the Ecase study conducted. These are essential for maintaining L the motivation of individuals in thCe development of projects since it makes them feel inserted into I T a work environment where mutual help and sharing of knowledge by team members thrive, R promoting high perforAmance in project development (Dwivedula and Bredillet, 2010; França et al., 2012). Regarding the rewards, working conditions, recognition, personal satisfaction, sense of accomplishment, and stability, these are also factors that were identified in the literature and our study and are essential for high motivation and, consequently, for high performance in the development of projects, since IS team members must feel that their work and their effort are valued. So, it is important that they feel satisfied with the overall progress of the project, with their work team, with the working conditions provided to them, and also with the recognition and ARTICLE IN PRESS rewards provided to them, thus contributing to high motivation (Benbya and Belbaly, 2010; Chen, Chern and Chen, 2012; Abdullah et al., 2016). Moreover, our study confirmed the following factors: challenging work, teamwork, self-efficacy, autonomy, problem-solving, and clarity of work goals. These motivation factors relate to team members’ perceptions of their work and what motivates them. Individuals must be able to plan their tasks and how they will carry them out, taking into account the level of difficulty that each task presents (Newton et al., 2002; França et al., 2020). S We have organized all the factors into five groups. The first group refers to the project, which S E addresses the way IS team members view certain characteristics of the work, such as, for example, R P the theme of the project in which they are involved and the role they play in it, among others. It N was observed that individuals prefer to be integrated into challenging work environments and I develop a ‘relevant’ project. The secoEnd group refers to project management, in which the L participants identified the need to Cwork on a well-organized project with rigorous planning of its I various phases. The third groTup is related to the support given to team members, both by their R teammates and by higher hierarchies, in the provision of information or elements that assist in the A development of the project. The greater the support provided, the higher the levels of motivation. The fourth group is related to the participants’ success in developing the project, which addresses the relevance of doing a successful job. Finally, the last group covers the importance of interpersonal relationships, whereby it was possible to understand that having empathic, friendly teammates who contribute to a good working environment is essential for motivation. ARTICLE IN PRESS 5.2 Contributions to practice and education The study of Saragih et al. (2021) argues that motivation is a stimulus for people to act according to the goals they have set, so it is essential to understand and identify the different factors that promote motivation. Our findings provide an important tool for institutions, organizations, and practitioners since they can use the results obtained in this work to aid in constructing and implementing individual motivation programs. Managers must diagnose their projects’ current situation concerning the factors identified here. Based on this diagnosis, it becomes possible to S implement training or teambuilding programs to improve the conditions that lead to high S E motivation, seeking to enhance the performance of projects. Furthermore, projects proposed in R educational settings (such as master courses) should Pbe defined considering the identified factors N to enhance students’ motivation and leverage learning results. I E 6. Conclusion L C Research on motivation has prodIuced important insights for the characterization of the factors that T R influence the motivation of project participants. However, the same is not true regarding the A motivation of IS project team members, particularly young professionals. To fill this gap, this paper presents the factors influencing young individuals’ motivation in IS projects, resulting from a survey of IS project participants. Throughout the development of this work, important influencers of motivation were identified; however, our study is not without limitations. One limitation is related to the fact that the survey occurred in projects carried out in the same academic setting, limiting its generalization so that, as future work, the study should be repeated in other contexts. Furthermore, since the study had as its main focus the motivation factors of individuals involved in IS projects, an in-depth study on the ARTICLE IN PRESS factors that contribute to the demotivation of individuals (“the other side of the coin”) is recommended as future work. JSON: Name: young_is_motivators_survey Title: Mixed-methods survey analysis of motivating factors for young professionals involved in information systems projects Short Hypothesis: Among young information-systems project team members, increases in intrinsic personality-trait scores (e.g., empathy and enjoyment of interaction) produce larger positive changes in individual motivation scores than equivalent increases in measured extrinsic reward levels. Related Work: Prior work on motivation in software engineering and information-systems projects has used systematic literature reviews, single-organization case studies, cross-sectional questionnaires, and qualitative analyses of project teams. These studies identify many candidate motivators (intrinsic task characteristics, autonomy, career development, leadership, work environment, rewards, communication, and team engagement) and show associations between motivation and performance. Limitations of existing approaches include: (1) aggregating across career stages and failing to isolate young professionals as a distinct population; (2) reliance on single-institution or single-company samples that limit external validity; (3) predominantly cross-sectional designs with limited use of hierarchical/mixed-effects models to control team- and year-level clustering; (4) heavy dependence on self-report measures without standardized personality or reward instruments; (5) sparse investigation of the project role (e.g., project manager versus analyst) as an independent motivator; and (6) few studies combining qualitative thematic coding with quantitative predictive modeling or ablation analyses to compare the relative explanatory power of intrinsic traits versus extrinsic incentives. Abstract: This study examines which factors most strongly drive motivation among young professionals participating in information-systems (IS) projects. Using a mixed-methods approach, we combine thematic coding of open-ended survey responses from project-based course participants with quantitative modeling of standardized survey measures (personality trait scales, intrinsic-extrinsic motivation inventories, role indicators, and reward metrics). The main contribution is a comparative analysis that quantifies the relative effect sizes of intrinsic personality traits, extrinsic rewards, and the role played in the project on individual motivation while accounting for team- and year-level clustering. We present predictive models (hierarchical linear models and machine-learning regressors) and ablation studies that evaluate how removing each factor class affects model performance and effect estimates. Expected outcomes include ranked predictors of motivation for young IS professionals and evidence on whether personality-based intrinsic factors dominate extrinsic incentives in this population. Results will inform project staffing, training priorities, and educational design for cultivating motivated early-career IS contributors. Experiments: Datasets: (A) Existing academic dataset: 931 anonymized survey responses collected 2014–2023 from semester-long IS projects (team size 3–6) including open answers and basic demographic/project metadata; (B) External replication dataset: collect N>=600 responses from young IS consultants (<=10 years experience) across >=3 consulting firms, including team identifiers and project domains. Measures: standardized Big Five or targeted subscales for empathy/interaction-enjoyment; Intrinsic Motivation Inventory (IMI) subscales; extrinsic reward index (pay grade proxies, formal recognition, grade/evaluation as applicable); role indicator (categorical: project manager, technical implementer, analyst, trainee); control covariates (age, gender, prior teamwork, project domain, pandemic period). Baselines: Baseline-1: extrinsic-only linear regression predicting continuous motivation score; Baseline-2: intrinsic-only linear regression; Baseline-3: role-only model; Proposed Model: hierarchical linear model (HLM) with fixed effects for intrinsic, extrinsic, role and interaction terms, random intercepts for team and year; ML baseline: random forest regressor using same predictors. Preprocessing: impute missing via multiple imputation (MICE), standardize continuous predictors, encode categorical variables. Experimental setup: split data by team into train (80%) / test (20%) preserving team clusters; perform 10-fold cross-validation on train; fit HLM with random intercepts for team and year and compare to ordinary least squares; test interaction terms between personality and role and between extrinsic rewards and role. Evaluation metrics: adjusted R^2, cross-validated R^2, RMSE, MAE, AIC/BIC for model comparison, intraclass correlation (ICC) for team/year variance, standardized effect sizes (beta coefficients) and p-values (alpha=0.05). Ablation studies: (i) drop personality predictors and record delta in test R^2 and change in key coefficients; (ii) drop extrinsic predictors; (iii) drop role indicator; (iv) remove random effects to quantify team/year clustering impact. Robustness checks: stratified analyses by pandemic period and by project domain; sensitivity analysis for multicollinearity (VIF>5). Statistical tests: likelihood-ratio tests comparing nested models and bootstrapped confidence intervals (n=2000) for effect estimates. Power analysis: ensure sample size yields >=80% power to detect small-to-moderate standardized effect (Cohen's f2=0.05) in mixed model given expected ICCs. Risk Factors and Limitations: Measurement bias: reliance on self-reported motivation and self-assessed personality traits introduces common-method and social-desirability bias. Sample bias: primary dataset originates from a single university course and may not represent broader cultural or industry contexts; replication dataset collection may face nonresponse and selection bias. Confounding: unmeasured variables (prior intrinsic interest, socioeconomic status, external job offers) may confound observed associations, limiting causal interpretation. Temporal effects: pandemic-related remote work may alter motivational dynamics and reduce comparability across years. Statistical issues: multicollinearity among predictors (e.g., personality and intrinsic motivation measures) can inflate variance of estimates; small effect sizes may require larger samples to detect. Generalization limits: findings may not generalize to senior professionals, other countries, or differing project types. Causal inference limits: observational survey data and cross-sectional designs constrain causal claims; instrumental variables or randomized assignment would be required for definitive causation. Data governance: access to external firm data may be restricted by confidentiality and GDPR constraints.
